system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-04-04 17:57:00 to 2175-04-07 12:43:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted with right leg cellulitis and fever after incomplete response to oral antibiotics. He was started on IV vancomycin, which was adjusted based on trough levels. Imaging ruled out DVT and fractures. His infection improved during the short hospital stay, and he was discharged home with a plan to complete a 10-day course of IV vancomycin during dialysis sessions. He was advised to continue all home medications, including those for gout, coronary artery disease, and hypertension, and to follow up with his primary care provider regarding medication adherence.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery

procedures.long_title: Insertion of drug-eluting coronary artery stent(s)

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in because of chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I had a little pain last night while watching TV. Just a tightness in my left chest. It went away after a few minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And then it happened again today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. After my dialysis, I got the same pain, but stronger. I also felt short of breath, dizzy, and a bit nauseous. They gave me a nitroglycerin pill under my tongue and it went away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re concerned this could be unstable angina—chest pain from your heart not getting enough blood. Your EKG showed some changes, and your troponin was slightly elevated, though not above your usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had stents before. In my right coronary artery. I haven’t had pain like this since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Given your history, we’re worried there might be some narrowing again in that stent. We’ll do a stress test tomorrow to check blood flow to your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? I’m on dialysis three times a week—Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stress test uses medication to simulate exercise. It’s not painful. And we’ve coordinated with the renal team—you’ll get dialysis tomorrow as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My potassium was high last time. I don’t want any issues with my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your potassium—it was 5.4, a bit high. We gave you Kayexalate to bring it down safely before any procedures. Your heart rhythm looks stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stress test results are back. There’s a new reversible defect in the inferior wall of your heart—this suggests reduced blood flow, likely due to restenosis in your old stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s narrowed again? What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend a cardiac catheterization. We’ll go in through your wrist or groin to look at the arteries and, if needed, reopen the blockage and place a new stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe with my dialysis access? I had angioplasty on my graft recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use your right femoral artery. Your graft is on the right arm, so it won’t interfere. We’ll also give contrast dye, but you’ll get dialysis afterward to clear it quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. We’ll admit you for monitoring tonight. You’ll stay overnight, get dialysis in the morning, then go straight to the cath lab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications? I take atenolol, aspirin, Plavix, simvastatin…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep taking aspirin and Plavix—those are crucial. We’re switching you from atenolol to Toprol XL 100 mg daily—it’s similar but better studied in your situation. And we’re adding lisinopril for blood pressure and heart protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So stop atenolol, start Toprol and lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll make sure the pharmacy sends those home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re scheduled for dialysis in an hour, then the cath lab at noon. Any chest pain overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None. I feel fine. Just a little anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The team will monitor you closely. The procedure usually takes about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. The cath showed restenosis in your old stent and a new blockage downstream. We ballooned the old area and placed a new drug-eluting stent. Blood flow is now excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Did everything go smoothly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfectly. No complications. Your heart enzymes didn’t rise afterward, which means no damage. You’ll stay overnight for observation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis? I’m due tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You already had it today—right after the procedure. We did it early to clear the contrast dye and reduce fluid load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I didn’t even feel it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the team coordinated it seamlessly. You’ll be on dual antiplatelet therapy—aspirin and clopidogrel—for at least a year to prevent stent clotting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on those before. Any changes to my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We lowered your simvastatin from 80 mg to 40 mg due to interactions with other meds. Cinacalcet was reduced to 30 mg twice daily. And sevelamer dose increased to control phosphorus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my gout medicine—allopurinol—I should keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue allopurinol. No changes there. Your foot pain limits walking, so keep using your cane.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today. You’ll need someone to drive you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us immediately if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or bleeding. Also, your cardiologist has changed—Dr. ___ will follow you now. Call to schedule an appointment in one month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your meds as prescribed, attend dialysis, and take it easy for a few days. You’ve been through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re glad we could help.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for evaluation of recurrent chest pain occurring at rest and after dialysis. Initial workup revealed nonspecific EKG changes and a stable, baseline-elevated troponin. A dipyridamole nuclear stress test showed a new reversible perfusion defect in the inferior wall, suggesting restenosis of a prior coronary stent. The patient underwent cardiac catheterization, which confirmed in-stent restenosis in the right coronary artery, and successfully received a new drug-eluting stent. He remained stable post-procedure, completed a scheduled hemodialysis session, and was discharged home in good condition. Medication changes included switching from atenolol to Toprol XL, adding lisinopril, and adjusting simvastatin and cinacalcet doses. Follow-up was arranged with a new cardiologist.
